text: Social media platforms should be legally required to share data with independent researchers, because the public currently has to take the companies' word about their own effects. UN investigators concluded in 2018 that social media, above all Facebook, had played a determining role in the violence against the Rohingya in Myanmar, yet outsiders could only reconstruct what happened after the harm was done. Researcher access would let problems be detected earlier.

Governments should be cautious about banning platforms outright, because bans are blunt and often leave the underlying problem untouched. India banned TikTok and dozens of other Chinese apps in 2020 over security concerns, and rival short-video apps quickly filled the gap, so the scrolling habit continued while the debate about data practices ended. Targeted rules on how data is handled would do more than a ban.

Platforms should be forced to take responsibility for election ads. Foreign groups bought political ads before the 2016 US election, and millions of people saw them without knowing who had paid. Rules requiring clear labels on political ads would make this much harder.

In 2019, after the Christchurch mosque attacks were livestreamed on Facebook, New Zealand and France launched the Christchurch Call, which many governments and companies later joined. In 2021, Australia's news bargaining law led Facebook to briefly block news for Australian users. In 2024, a Brazilian Supreme Court justice ordered X to be suspended in the country.

Platforms should be legally required to stop the livestreaming of mass violence from spreading, because voluntary pledges arrive too late. After the 2019 Christchurch attacks were livestreamed on Facebook, the company removed well over a million copies of the video within the first day, but the sheer volume showed that removal after the fact is not enough. The Christchurch Call that governments and companies joined is voluntary, so binding duties for rapid detection and removal would go further.

Governments should leave social media largely alone and invest in educating users instead, because regulation tends to lag behind technology and often protects large firms. Big platforms can afford compliance teams that smaller competitors cannot, so heavy rules may entrench the very companies they are meant to restrain. Many experts believe media literacy is a better long-term investment.
